Keywords: Home, Geometry, Old

outputs.L1:
I was someone’s honor student once—a sticker, a star. I aced Home Ec and Geometry; I learned to wield a fork, to steer my mother’s car. Old enough to work, I refreshed the salad bar at Steak & Ale, scarcity a line I could not fail. In the summers between university terms, I interned at AT&T, in the minority outreach program they called Inroads. My boss, Vicki, had two roommates, whom she referred to simply as “The Gays,” crashing on her floor.

That was before I was gay, though I will not try to say that with a straight face. As if anyone really cares—yet I care. What I am trying to say is this: all of it prepared me for these squat, blinking office accessories. For the dry drinking after the accidental reply-all.

By now, there is a great deal to lose. Little by little, I have become so careful: no talk of politics, no mention of orientation. I let them say, “He’s a homosexual,” without offering an arch correction. At a fondue buffet in Zurich, our dumbfounded senior group director—when I let slip, damn it, my trip with a twenty-year-old—inquired, “They’re always over seventeen, right?” I told her, “Of course, God, yes,” and, seething, smiled, which I am famous for. I did not want to scare her.

But I tell you, I am keeping score. E-mail is no more than a suicide I would like to recall. Note my suicide. I am paid to multitask, to scramble the life out of fun: Monday I will ask—every dash a loaded gun, every comma a knife—that you bury the black-box file.
outputs.L2:
Once, I was the prized student in someone’s eyes—the gold sticker, the shining star. I got top marks in Home Economics and Geometry; I was taught how to jab properly with a fork and how to guide my mother’s car. When I was old enough to have a job, I kept the salad bar stocked at Steak & Ale, where running short was a mistake I couldn’t afford. During the summers between college terms, I worked as an intern at AT&T through the minority outreach program known as Inroads.

My supervisor, Vicki, had two people sleeping on her floor—roommates she referred to plainly as “The Gays.” This was before I was gay, though I can’t pretend to say that seriously. Maybe no one else cares, but I do. What I mean is that all of it somehow trained me for these low, blinking office machines, for the tense, dry drinking that follows an accidental reply-all email. At this point, there is too much at stake.

Gradually, I have learned to be extremely cautious. I avoid mentioning politics or sexual identity. When people call me “a homosexual,” I do not step in with a sharp correction. Once, at a fondue buffet in Zurich, after I stupidly mentioned a trip I’d taken with a twenty-year-old, our stunned senior group director asked whether they were always over seventeen. I assured her they were—of course, yes, absolutely—and smiled while furious inside, a smile I’m known for. I didn’t want to alarm her. Still, believe me, I am keeping count.

Email feels like nothing more than a self-destruction I wish I could take back. Please notice: my self-destruction. I am paid to juggle tasks, to drain all pleasure from life. On Monday, with every dash feeling like a cocked weapon and every comma like a blade, I will ask you to bury the black-box file.

The speaker looks back on a life shaped by achievement, discipline, and the ability to succeed within the roles expected of them. They have learned how to perform well in school, at work, and in professional spaces by understanding the rules—both spoken and unspoken. Their past is marked by accomplishment, but also by conformity: a steady process of adapting themselves to fit into institutions that reward politeness, ambition, and self-control.

Early jobs and internships teach the speaker how workplaces really function. They encounter hierarchies of power, subtle codes of behavior, and language that often conceals more than it reveals. In these environments, casual comments about gay people reveal the prejudices that can exist beneath a professional surface. The speaker learns that offices are not neutral spaces; they are places where people signal belonging, authority, and exclusion through jokes, assumptions, and offhand remarks.

As a result, the speaker becomes increasingly cautious at work. They learn to avoid subjects that might expose too much of themselves, especially politics or sexual orientation. Silence becomes a form of protection. Rather than risk conflict, judgment, or professional consequences, the speaker carefully manages what they say and how they appear. This caution reflects the emotional labor of navigating a workplace where being fully open may feel unsafe.

The speaker recalls specific moments of homophobia and discomfort in professional settings. In these situations, they respond outwardly with politeness, professionalism, and restraint. They smile, answer calmly, and continue doing what is expected of them. Inwardly, however, they remember each insult, slight, and coded comment. They keep score, registering the gap between the workplace’s surface civility and the prejudice that still circulates within it.

The poem presents office communication, especially email, as tense and potentially dangerous. Every message must be carefully written, because even ordinary words can carry risk. Tone, phrasing, and implication become matters of survival. Email is not simply a tool for efficiency; it is a record, a performance, and a possible weapon. In this world, professional language becomes charged with anxiety, and the speaker must constantly calculate the consequences of what they say and what they leave unsaid.

The poem presents a speaker looking back on a life shaped by ambition, adaptation, and restraint. Through autobiographical fragments, the speaker suggests that achievement has never been simple or uncomplicated. Success has required not only talent and effort, but also a constant process of self-management: choosing what to reveal, what to soften, what to hide, and what emotions must never be allowed to surface. The speaker’s life in professional spaces is therefore marked by assimilation. In order to belong, or at least to survive, the speaker has had to adopt the language, manners, and expectations of the workplace, even when those expectations demand the concealment of essential parts of the self.

The poem uses the imagery of office life—memos, meetings, emails, résumés, polished speech, and professional etiquette—to show how corporate culture can appear neutral while actually enforcing conformity. Ordinary workplace communication becomes charged with pressure. Every phrase must be measured; every response must be edited before it is spoken. The speaker cannot simply express anger, discomfort, desire, or pain. Instead, those feelings must be translated into acceptable professional language, if they can be expressed at all. This creates a form of self-censorship in which the speaker is always watching the self from the outside, anticipating judgment and avoiding exposure.

The poem also connects this restraint to the experience of homophobia. The speaker’s identity is not treated as something that can exist freely within the workplace. Rather, it becomes something potentially dangerous, something that might disrupt the smooth surface of professionalism. As a result, professionalism itself is shown to be political. It is not merely a code of competence or courtesy; it is also a system that rewards silence, emotional discipline, and the suppression of difference. The speaker’s anger is understandable, but the workplace requires that anger to be hidden, refined, or disguised. This enforced calm becomes exhausting.

By presenting these pressures through fragments of memory and corporate imagery, the poem reveals the psychological cost of survival in hostile or conformist environments. What may look from the outside like success is shown from within to involve vigilance and loss. The speaker has achieved, but achievement has come at the price of continual concealment. The poem ultimately argues that the violence of such spaces is not always dramatic or visible. It can take the form of ordinary language, polite expectations, and the daily demand to remain composed. In this way, the poem transforms the familiar world of professional communication into a site of psychic violence, exposing how deeply homophobia and conformity can shape a person’s inner life.
outputs.L5:
Home is more than a place with walls and a roof; it is a quiet geometry of memory. Every room has its own shape, every corner holds a story, and every doorway seems to measure the distance between who we were and who we have become.

In the old house, the lines were never perfectly straight. The wooden floor leaned slightly, the windows sat unevenly in their frames, and the ceiling seemed lower in winter when the light grew dim. Yet there was beauty in that imperfect geometry. The square kitchen table gathered generations around it. The narrow hallway connected laughter, footsteps, and whispers. The circular clock on the wall marked time, but it also preserved it.

As years passed, the home grew old, but not empty. Its angles softened with dust and sunlight. Its rooms became maps of family life, drawn not with rulers, but with love, loss, and belonging. Geometry may explain the shape of a house, but only memory can explain the meaning of a home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary confessional poem in the voice of a gay corporate office worker reflecting on childhood achievement, early jobs, code-switching at work, microaggressions, and the dread of email, with dark humor and enjambed lines.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inbox Zero**

As a child I collected certificates  
the way other boys collected bruises—  
laminated proof I was good  
at sitting still, at sounding white  
on the phone, at making adults  
temporarily less afraid  
of my future.

Most Improved. Perfect Attendance.  
A gold star for not screaming  
when the coach called me sweetheart  
like a dare.

My first job was bagging groceries  
for women who said, You’re so articulate,  
then handed me coupons damp  
with purse sweat. I learned to double-bag  
eggs, grief, anything fragile  
and not mine.

Then retail, where I folded sweaters  
into calm little coffins.  
Then the call center, where my name  
became shorter, rounder,  
less ethnic, less limp-wristed,  
more likely to be promoted  
by a man named Brad who kept saying  
we’re a family, which is how I knew  
someone was about to get sacrificed.

Now I work in a glass building  
that reflects the sky  
like it has shareholders.  
Every morning I badge in  
and assemble the version of myself  
with no visible seams:  
voice lowered, laugh rationed,  
wrists disciplined into corners.

In meetings I say bandwidth  
when I mean soul.  
I say alignment  
when I mean please stop interrupting me.  
I say circling back  
because murder is still illegal  
and HR has a wellness portal.

The straight men slap my shoulder  
like checking fruit.  
They ask if my weekend was fabulous  
as if fabulous is a location  
with mandatory brunch.  
A woman in finance says  
I just love how you say things,  
and I watch my mouth  
become an exhibit.

Once, during Pride month,  
they put a rainbow on the logo  
and cut dental.  
We all clapped in the atrium,  
our teeth shining with gratitude  
and future debt.

I am successful, technically.  
My calendar is a hostage situation.  
My childhood trophies gather dust  
in my mother’s basement,  
little gold men with no genitals  
raising their arms  
like they’ve survived something.

Maybe they have.

Every email arrives  
wearing a small black hood.  
Per my last message.  
Just checking in.  
Friendly reminder.  
Each subject line  
a coffin nail tapped in  
with managerial softness.

At night I dream of unread messages  
breeding in the walls,  
tiny red numbers multiplying  
like shame with a user interface.

I wake before dawn  
to the blue light of my phone,  
my face floating above it  
pale and available.

Dear Team, I type,  
then stop.

There is no team.  
There is only me  
and the old gifted child  
inside me, still raising his hand,  
still desperate to be chosen  
by anyone with the power  
to leave him alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem that begins with being an “honor student” and moves through Home Ec, Steak & Ale, an AT&T internship, closeted office culture, an awkward Zurich business dinner, and ends with a bleak metaphor about email and a “black-box file.”
counterfactuals.output:
Honor student,  
I learned early how to fold myself  
into the clean margins of a page,  
how to answer before being asked,  
how to keep my hands visible  
and my hunger hidden.

In Home Ec we stitched aprons  
from stiff cotton,  
measured flour with the seriousness  
of pharmacists,  
learned that a household  
could be managed  
if you followed the recipe  
and never named  
what was burning.

At Steak & Ale,  
under the dim fake-Tudor lights,  
I carried plates like small economies—  
sirloin, baked potato, sour cream  
in its pleated paper cup—  
and smiled until my face  
felt rented.

Then AT&T,  
the internship badge clipped to my chest  
like proof of a future.  
I practiced the language of terminals,  
conference rooms,  
deliverables,  
men who spoke in acronyms  
and laughed at jokes  
that had no door in them  
for me to leave through.

The office was closeted  
in the old way:  
not silent, exactly,  
but upholstered in denial.  
Everyone knew  
which pronouns to misplace,  
which invitations not to extend,  
which photographs were safe  
to set on a desk.  
Desire became a typo  
we were paid to correct.

Years later, Zurich—  
a business dinner too polished  
to touch.  
White linen, lake-dark windows,  
forks arranged like an exam.  
Someone ordered wine  
with the confidence  
of inherited weather.  
I told a story that landed wrong,  
then watched it lie there  
between the veal and the mineral water,  
small and breathing.

All that ambition,  
all that careful passing  
through rooms with fluorescent ceilings,  
and still the day narrows  
to a screen refreshing itself  
without mercy.

Email falls and falls,  
gray sleet in the inbox,  
each message another corridor  
with no window,  
each attachment sealed,  
unreadable,  
waiting at the bottom of the system  
like a black-box file  
recovered from a crash  
no one survived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poem in the style of a late-20th-century American narrative poet: witty, bitter, autobiographical, queer, and office-bound. Include corporate travel, reply-all anxiety, careful punctuation, and the speaker silently keeping score.
counterfactuals.output:
**Expense Report with Minor Injuries**

At 6:10 a.m., the airport was already  
performing its little opera of compliance:  
belts unbuckled, laptops unsheathed,  
everyone briefly made equal  
by the possibility of shampoo.

I was traveling for the firm—  
“firm” being the word we used  
for the thing that softened us.  
In Omaha, or maybe Charlotte,  
I gave the same presentation  
I had given in Phoenix,  
with one joke improved  
and one silence allowed to live.

The client laughed in the wrong place.  
I marked it down.

Back at my desk, after the return flight  
and its medicinal pretzels,  
there it was: the thread.

Subject: Re: Re: Re: Quick Question

A bloom of names, blue and prosecutorial.  
Someone had replied all  
to correct “principle” to “principal,”  
and now the whole floor breathed  
with the tender panic  
of people who had opinions  
but mortgages.

I typed: Thanks, all—  
then stopped.

The dash looked needy.  
The comma looked weak.  
The period, frankly, was hostile.  
I deleted everything  
and sat very still,  
as if stillness were a form  
of leadership.

Across the aisle, Mark told Stacy  
about his wife’s gluten thing.  
Stacy said, Wow.  
I gave Stacy a point  
for tonal restraint  
and subtracted two from Mark  
for “thing.”

This was how I survived:  
not nobly, not even well,  
but with a private ledger  
kept in the smallest handwriting—  
one for the analyst  
who said “circle back” six times  
before lunch,  
one against the VP  
who touched my shoulder  
while praising “diversity,”  
three for the receptionist  
who called me honey  
as if she meant  
you poor beautiful clerk  
of your own diminishment.

At the hotel bar in Dallas,  
a man in a lanyard asked  
what line I was in.  
I said, Mostly dotted.  
He did not deserve that,  
but I gave it to him.

Later, upstairs,  
I hung my suit in the bathroom  
and let the shower steam  
worry the wrinkles out.  
My face in the mirror  
looked promoted beyond its training.

There were messages from my mother,  
who had learned to say partner  
with the careful emphasis  
of a tourist ordering soup abroad.  
There was one from him—  
lowercase, affectionate, brief—  
which I read twice  
and answered once,  
with punctuation so exact  
it could have passed  
for distance.

By Friday, the office had forgiven  
or forgotten the reply-all incident.  
New emergencies rose  
like weather over cubicles.  
Someone’s badge stopped working.  
Someone’s numbers were “directional.”  
Someone brought cupcakes  
for a birthday nobody could place.

I ate one at my desk,  
vanilla, unremarkable, free,  
and added it to the score:  
world, one;  
me, still counting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary monologue from the perspective of someone who has spent their life learning to behave properly—school, service jobs, internships, corporate work—while hiding anger about homophobia in professional settings.
counterfactuals.output:
I have always known where to put my hands.

Folded on the desk. Flat on the counter. Lightly clasped in front of me during the interview, wrists relaxed, no fidgeting. Hands say so much, they told us—at school, at training, at the seminar about executive presence—hands can betray you. So I trained mine not to. I trained my face, too. I learned to receive insults like weather.

At school I learned posture first. Sit up straight. Don’t talk back. Don’t make everything about yourself. When the boys behind me whispered that word—soft as spit, sharp as a pin—I learned the correct response was not to turn around. Turning around was disruption. Turning around made it an incident. Better to prove them wrong by being excellent, quiet, and clean. Better to become the kind of child adults praised in staff rooms: mature, composed, no trouble at all.

No trouble at all. That was my first profession.

Later, in service jobs, I learned the customer is always right, even when he watches the way your eyes follow a man across the room and smiles like he has discovered contraband. Even when she asks, in front of the register line, whether you have a girlfriend, then laughs too long when you say no. I learned to polish glasses, bag groceries, carry plates, apologize for delays I did not cause. I learned that humiliation can be laminated into a name tag. That it can smell like fryer oil and floor cleaner. That it can wear a lanyard and say, “We’re like family here.”

Families, I had already noticed, were the first institutions where people practiced deniability.

Then came internships, where I discovered a higher class of cruelty: ergonomic, softly lit, buffered by policy. No one said the word outright there. They didn’t have to. They said fit. They said culture. They said client-facing. They said, “You’ll understand when you’ve been here longer.” They lowered their voices near me and raised them when talking about their wives, husbands, weekends at wineries, children with jam on their faces. They decorated their desks with the evidence of approved love and called it personality. I kept my desk clear.

I became fluent in the grammar of withholding.

On Monday mornings, I knew how to edit my weekend into acceptable shapes. I saw a movie. I met a friend. I stayed in. Never: I woke beside him and watched the sun move over his shoulder like a hand learning tenderness. Never: we argued in the cereal aisle, then laughed on the bus home. Never: his mother called and called and he did not answer because love, in some families, arrives dressed as a threat.

No, I saw a movie. I met a friend. I stayed in.

In corporate work, propriety became architecture. Glass walls, conference rooms named after mountains, a kitchenette where people rinsed mugs and reputations. There were trainings about inclusion with stock photographs of smiling minorities, but the laughter at lunch still knew where to land. Someone’s brother-in-law was “basically a woman.” Someone’s college roommate was “a little too interested” in the team. Someone lowered their voice to tell a story about a client’s “lifestyle,” and everyone leaned in as if disgust were confidential information.

And there I was, nodding at the correct intervals. Producing reports. Meeting deadlines. Saying “Great question” to men who had mistaken volume for thought. Saying “No worries” to women who worried very little. Saying “I appreciate the feedback” to people who meant, Be less visible in ways I can’t legally name.

Do you know what anger does when it is not allowed to become sound?

It organizes.

Mine built shelves inside me. It filed every joke, every glance, every sudden silence after I entered the room. It kept minutes of meetings no one else remembered. It preserved the exact temperature of the air when a manager said, “Of course we support everyone, but some clients are more traditional.” It cataloged the smile I used in response: modest, grateful, nearly dead.

For years I believed professionalism meant making myself easy to survive. I dressed in neutral colors. I laughed at half volume. I answered emails with exclamation points like little flags of surrender. Happy to help! Sounds good! No problem at all!

There was always a problem.

The problem was not that I was offended. Offense is too small a word, too decorative, like a vase placed over a crack in the foundation. The problem was that I was being asked, over and over, to collaborate in my own erasure and call it maturity. To understand that my dignity was conditional upon everyone else’s comfort. To treat each small wound as a misunderstanding, each pattern as coincidence, each insult as a chance to demonstrate resilience.

Resilience. Another word they loved. They admired resilience the way people admire a bridge after they overload it.

I have been praised for my calm by people who made it necessary. I have been called gracious by those who benefited from my silence. I have been invited to bring my whole self to work by people who flinched at the first honest sentence.

My whole self. Imagine the audacity of that invitation. As if the self were a lunch packed neatly in the morning: apple, sandwich, napkin folded. As if I could set it on the conference table between the quarterly forecasts and the branded pens. As if my whole self had not been frisked at the door of every room I entered.

And still—I behaved. I knew how to behave.

I knew how to lower my voice when talking about my life. I knew how to say partner only after someone else said it first. I knew how to scan a room for danger while appearing to look for a seat. I knew which colleagues could be trusted with a pronoun and which required a fog of nouns: person, someone, friend. I knew how to make my anger urbane. How to put a blazer on it. How to send it to meetings with action items.

But lately my hands have begun to forget their training.

They curl under tables. They open and close. They want to point, to strike wood, to tear the neat agenda in half. My face, that old employee of the month, has started missing shifts. Something true keeps rising through it.

I am tired of being reasonable in unreasonable rooms.

I am tired of the little administrative tasks of concealment, the constant revisions, the emotional expense reports no one reimburses. I am tired of watching cowards congratulate themselves for tolerance because they have learned not to say the ugliest thing aloud. I am tired of professionalism being used as a velvet rope around other people’s prejudice.

What I want to say is: I heard you.

All of you.

I heard what you meant when you joked. I heard what you feared when you cautioned me to be discreet. I heard the verdict inside your advice. I heard the old machinery humming beneath the new language. I heard my name being replaced by category, my love by issue, my anger by attitude.

And I want, just once, not to translate myself into something harmless.

I want to enter a room and let the room become responsible for what it does with me. I want to stop smoothing the tablecloth over the rot. I want to speak plainly and watch politeness panic. I want to say that I have spent my life being trained for a world that was never trained to receive me.

But here is the terrible part: even now, even with all this fire in my mouth, I can still feel the old lessons arranging me. Keep it measured. Keep it strategic. Don’t burn bridges. Don’t make them uncomfortable. Don’t give them a reason.

As if they ever needed one.

So let this be improper, then. Let it arrive without the right tone. Let it miss the meeting invite, ignore the dress code, interrupt the speaker. Let it be documented. Let it go on the record.

I was not calm. I was careful.

I was not gracious. I was outnumbered.

I was not professional. I was surviving.

And all that time, beneath the folded hands and the neutral shirts, beneath the customer-service smile and the polished résumé, beneath every “happy to help” and “no problem at all,” I was angry.

I am angry still.

Only now I am learning to put my hands wherever I like.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly funny free verse poem about workplace self-censorship and being gay in corporate America, using specific details like Steak & Ale, Inroads at AT&T, “The Gays,” a fondue buffet in Zurich, and the phrase “every comma, a knife.”
counterfactuals.output:
At the lunch-and-learn on Authenticity  
we were each handed a branded pen  
and a paper cup of grapes.

I wrote **team player**  
where the form asked for identity,  
because HR was smiling  
like a motion sensor light  
outside a garage where something has died.

Inroads at AT&T taught me early  
how to translate myself  
into something with a tie clip.

Say “roommate,” not “boyfriend.”  
Say “weekend plans,” not “Pride.”  
Say “diverse perspectives,” not  
I have measured the width of my laugh  
against the glass walls of conference rooms  
and found it too wide.

At Steak & Ale, years ago,  
under the medieval lamps  
and the fake Tudor beams,  
I watched a regional manager  
cut into prime rib  
and announce he had no problem with The Gays,  
capital T, capital G,  
as if we were a product line  
being test-marketed in Dallas.

Everyone nodded.  
The baked potatoes steamed  
like tiny hostage situations.

I learned to edit in real time:  
my hands, my earrings, my pronouns,  
the song I knew all the words to,  
the obituary tone I used  
when mentioning “a friend”  
who had in fact shared my bed  
and my dental insurance anxieties.

Corporate America loves a clean sentence.  
No dangling modifiers.  
No sudden softness.  
No anecdote that ends  
with two men kissing in a cab  
outside the Marriott.

Before sending any email  
I searched for evidence of myself:  
too much exclamation,  
too much warmth,  
the word “fabulous” standing near a budget number  
like a drag queen at a compliance seminar.

Track Changes became my confessional.  
Delete.  
Delete.  
Rephrase.  
Every comma, a knife.

Once, in Zurich,  
at a fondue buffet  
paid for by Global Sales Enablement,  
I watched vice presidents spear bread cubes  
and lower them into molten cheese  
with the solemnity of war criminals.

Outside, the Alps looked innocent.  
Inside, someone asked if my wife  
enjoyed traveling.

I said, “She’s more of a homebody,”  
which was true  
if “she” meant my fear,  
and “homebody” meant  
it had moved into my chest  
and started forwarding mail.

How funny,  
the tiny costumes survival gives us.

The navy blazer.  
The neutral ringtone.  
The laugh calibrated  
to suggest heterosexual golf.

How hilarious  
to sit through another panel  
on bringing your whole self to work  
while your whole self waits downstairs  
by the loading dock,  
smoking,  
wearing eyeliner,  
refusing to badge in.

I have been praised  
for my professionalism,  
which is to say  
for my ability to bleed  
without getting it on the spreadsheet.

I have been called articulate  
by men who meant  
thank you for not making this awkward.

I have been invited to speak  
during Pride Month  
for seven minutes  
between a cybersecurity update  
and sheet cake.

There is a rainbow logo  
in the lobby now.  
There are pronouns in some signatures.  
There is a mentoring circle  
called Belonging  
that meets on Thursdays  
in a room named after a dead founder  
who probably would have fired us all.

Still, I draft my life carefully.

Still, before I say “we,”  
I look for exits.

Still, I can make a joke  
so dry it passes legal review.

Still, somewhere in the building,  
The Gays are circulating—  
unconfirmed, high-performing,  
excellent with clients,  
quietly saving the deck  
while the network drive collapses.

We are in the footnotes,  
the margins,  
the tasteful scarf,  
the immaculate pivot table,  
the sudden silence  
after someone says  
“not that there’s anything wrong with it”  
and waits to be absolved  
by the nearest homosexual.

Bless them,  
for they know exactly what they do.

Bless the conference badges,  
the airport bars,  
the mandatory fun,  
the anonymous survey  
where I almost told the truth  
but chose “somewhat agree.”

Bless Steak & Ale,  
with its dark booths  
where I swallowed my own name  
beside the horseradish.

Bless Inroads at AT&T,  
where I learned the phone voice  
that could sell long distance  
and long suffering.

Bless Zurich,  
where the cheese kept bubbling  
like a golden, corporate hell  
and I raised my glass  
to synergy,  
to plausible deniability,  
to the career-saving art  
of becoming a person  
only after 6 p.m.

And bless my mouth,  
that little office  
with no windows,  
still opening  
for business.
